Retrying HTTP requests without making things worse

By Dana Whitfield · March 4, 2026

Retries look harmless. A request fails, you send it again, and most of the time the second attempt works. The trouble starts when every client does the same thing at the same moment: a short outage turns into a long one because the recovering server is flooded with retries.

This post walks through the three rules we now follow in every service. None of them is new, but writing them down made our reviews faster. If you only read one section, read the one about budgets.

Rule 1: back off exponentially, with jitter

Wait longer after each failure, and add randomness so that clients spread out. The full-jitter variant picks a delay uniformly between zero and the current cap:

fn delay(attempt: u32, base_ms: u64, cap_ms: u64) -> u64 {
    let ceiling = cap_ms.min(base_ms << attempt);
    rand::random::<u64>() % (ceiling + 1)
}

We use base_ms = 100 and cap_ms = 10_000 for interactive calls.

Rule 2: only retry what is safe to repeat

A retry is a second copy of the request. That is fine for reads and for writes that carry an idempotency key, and dangerous for everything else.

  • Retry GET, HEAD and PUT freely.
  • Retry POST only with an Idempotency-Key header.
  • Never retry on 400 or 422: the request itself is wrong.

Rule 3: keep a retry budget

Cap retries at a fraction of normal traffic, for example ten percent over a rolling minute. When the budget is spent, fail fast and let the caller decide.

A retry budget turns a thundering herd into a polite queue.

StatusRetry?Honour Retry-After?
429yesyes

500with budgetno

More background is in our earlier post on choosing timeouts and in the Retry-After section of RFC 9110.
